Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

premise noun

what an argument starts from

also premises (of an argument), starting point (of an argument), major premise, minor premise

classical

Cic. Div. 2.108 (Lewis & Short)

sūmptiō, sūmptiōnis f.

noun, third declension

a premise taken for granted

Lewis & Short: “in logic, a premise taken for granted, an assumption”. A rare word: in conversation the premise is what has been laid down, quod positum est (see assumption), or the foundation, fundāmentum.

Other words

  • prōpositiō, prōpositiōnis f. — the first premise of a syllogism

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Inv. 1.67 (Lewis & Short)

    A term of logic, paired with assūmptiō, the second premise. Outside logic prōpositiō is a setting forth, a theme or a purpose (Lewis & Short).

  • assūmptiō, assūmptiōnis f. — the second (minor) premise of a syllogism

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Inv. 1.64; Div. 2.108 (Lewis & Short)

    A term of logic only; in later Latin a taking up, and in the Church the Assumption.

  • fundāmentum, fundāmentī n. — foundation, basis

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 1.23: fundāmentum autem est jūstitiae fidēs

    Literally the foundation of a building; figuratively the ground a thing rests on (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • prōpositiō est, per quam locus is breviter expōnitur, ex quō vīs omnis oportet ēmānet ratiōcinātiōnis

    the first premise is the statement that briefly sets out the point from which the whole force of the reasoning must flowCic. Inv. 1.67 (Lewis & Short)

  • fundāmentum autem est jūstitiae fidēs, id est dictōrum conventōrumque cōnstantia et vēritās

    the foundation of justice is good faith, that is, keeping to what has been said and agreed, and truthfulnessCic. Off. 1.23

See also assumption, assume, argument.
